title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
summary: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. content:
Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a
kilonova
. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s
Kilonova Catcher
project!
Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When
gravitational wave
detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.
The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar
Impact Flash!
project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new
Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope
.
“Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.”
The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”
To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit
https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/
or send an email to
kilonovacatcher@gmail.com
. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!
On Aug. 17, 2017, the
Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory
(LIGO) and the
Virgo Interferometer
both detected gravitational waves from the collision between two neutron stars. Within 12 hours observatories had identified the source of the event within the lenticular galaxy NGC 4993, shown in this image, which was gathered with NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. The associated kilonova is clearly visible in the Hubble observations. This is the first time the optical counterpart of a gravitational wave event was observed. Hubble observed the kilonova gradually fading over the course of six days, as illustrated by the three time-stamped inset images made between Aug. 22 and 28.

title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
summary: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during […]
content:
Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.
From left, technicians Chad Cook and Seth Harvey install the high-resolution microscopic imager – part of the seven-camera DragonCam science imaging suite – onto NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, on Nov. 6, 2026.
NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Ed Whitman
First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize
Titan
’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground. By mid-November, all seven cameras developed and built by Malin Space Science Systems had been installed in their insulated housings, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft. Each camera will look out at Titan through a window in a foam enclosure that insulates the cameras and Dragonfly’s interior from Titan’s cryogenic environment, where ambient temperatures reach minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit.
A configurable LED array, built at APL and spanning the light spectrum from the infrared to the ultraviolet, provides information about the color of surface materials at the sampling site and helps scientists make inferences about their composition. During Titan’s long night, which spans nearly eight Earth days, these observations also may allow DragonCam to identify organic molecules that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The LED illumination also allows us to see Titan as human eyes would.
“One of the most exciting things about Dragonfly is that we’ll be able to see Titan from perspectives we’ve never had before,” said Elizabeth Turtle, Dragonfly principal investigator at APL. “With the capability to take images when Dragonfly is on the surface as well as while flying, DragonCam will give us both detailed views and sweeping panoramas of Titan’s landscape, as well as insight into the processes that shaped this extraordinary world. Seeing these cameras become part of the Dragonfly lander is an exciting milestone that brings us another step closer to this unprecedented exploration.”
Matthew Clark (left) and Michael Ravine of Malin Space Science Systems check DragonCam’s seven science cameras and digital video recorder before shipping them to Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) for integration and testing onto NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft.
MSSS/Olawale Oluwo
In addition to these science cameras, Dragonfly has two navigation cameras, also built by Malin Space Science Systems, that were installed this summer.
“We are extremely pleased to have delivered the DragonCam cameras,” said Michael Ravine, DragonCam development manager and a Dragonfly co-investigator from Malin Space Science Systems.  “Now to have them on the Dragonfly spacecraft, taking images, it’s so much easier to picture how they will work on Titan. These will be our eyes to see and explore this whole new world.”
Two forward-mounted cameras — a wide-angle camera (WAC) and medium-angle camera (MAC) — are designed to capture images of the terrain in front of Dragonfly. The forward WAC offers a 90-degree field of view, while the forward MAC overlaps with the WAC, capturing part of that field of view at a higher resolution. Combined, the images from these two cameras provide a stereoscopic perspective from the front of the lander. Together with two additional side-mounted WACs, the system is able to capture panoramic views of the Titan landscape.
Panoramic view of the cleanroom at APL, Johns Hopkins APL, consisting of three images taken by Dragonfly’s forward- and side-facing wide-angle cameras (WACs). At left is Dragonfly’s top deck, including its circular high-gain antenna (seen edge-on), and members of the APL and Malin Space Science Systems integration and testing team are visible in the control room windows. The images – taken on Nov. 9, 2026, shortly after the DragonCam camera suite was installed on the lander – have a yellow tint because DragonCam captures light differently than the human eye sees it.
NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/MSSS
Two downward-facing WACs provide views of the surface beneath Dragonfly, helping the mission team decide if a landing spot is safe for deploying Dragonfly’s sample-collecting tool, known as DrACO, or Drill for Acquisition of Complex Organics, and its seismometer. A high-resolution microscopic imager will aim at DrACO’s drill site to pick out the details in millimeter-sized sand grains around the sampling location.
“DragonCam will give us critical context for the samples collected by DrACO,” said Carolyn Ernst, the DragonCam instrument scientist at APL. “We’ll be collecting materials at multiple sites across Titan, and the images from the cameras will help us relate the samples to Titan’s broader landscape and piece together the story of its geology.”
DragonCam is a suite of cameras aboard NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft designed to capture images of Titan’s surface from the ground and during flight. DragonCam will help scientists study landforms and surface processes at multiple scales, providing new insights into Titan’s geology and environment. This animation highlights the elements of DragonCam and how its imaging capabilities will support Dragonfly’s scientific investigations
NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Zac Swanson
Components of Dragonfly’s other
instrument packages
, DraGNS (Gamma-ray and Neutron Spectrometer), DraGMet (Geophysics and Meteorology), DraMS (Mass Spectrometer) and DrACO, are set for delivery, integration and testing over the next several months. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034.

title: NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
summary: The brilliant galaxy NGC 4394 with its distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this Hubble Space Telescope image
content:
3 min read
NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
The brilliant galaxy NGC 4394 with its distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image.
ESA/Hubble & NASA, E. Peng, D. Thilker and the MAUVE-HST Team
A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice’s Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It’s one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us.
With its graceful spiral arms and central bar of stars, NGC 4394 closely resembles what astronomers think our home galaxy, the Milky Way, would look like if we were able to view it from a similar face-on vantage point. In a universe full of arcing spiral galaxies and nebulae organically shaped by the death and birth of stars, straight streaks of stars like NGC 4394’s galactic bar stand out. Galactic bars are extremely common; astronomers estimate 65 percent of nearby spiral galaxies have one. Hubble has imaged a wide variety of stunning barred spiral galaxies, including
NGC 5728
,
NGC 685
, and
NGC 613
, but how do these striking features form?
Explanations for how galactic bars might form tend to center on a galaxy’s disk of stars becoming unstable. This could happen because of gravitational nudges from passing galaxies, interactions between stars, or other forces. Once the disk becomes unstable, the circular orbits of stars become elongated, leading to the barred shape seen in galaxies like NGC 4394. Observations show that galactic bars are more common among galaxies in the universe today than they were several billion years ago. Though stellar bars are in fashion today, research suggests that this is only temporary; as bars become more massive, they can themselves become unstable.
In addition to their stellar bars and spiral arms, NGC 4394 and the Milky Way galaxy share another important similarity, in that they might both contain a LINER (low-ionization nuclear emission-line region). LINER refers to an area near the center of a galaxy where its spectra feature certain ionized or neutral elements. Researchers do not yet know exactly how LINERs form, though either hungry supermassive black holes or intense star formation likely play a role.
Hubble has paid a visit to NGC 4394’s patch of sky more than once, and a
previous image of NGC 4394
was released a decade ago. That image was part of an observing program (#
10515
; PI: Peng) that focused on NGC 4394’s galactic neighbor,
Messier 85
. While one of Hubble’s instruments examined Messier 85 to study its unusual collection of star clusters, another (Hubble’s
Advanced Camera for Surveys
) captured a parallel area of the sky that contained NGC 4394.
Today’s image also incorporates observations from a recent program (#
18103
; PI: Thilker) dedicated to understanding how star formation comes to an end in galaxies in dense cluster environments, and how this process differs from more isolated galaxies adrift in the field. For this observing program, researchers used Hubble’s
Wide Field Camera 3
and its sensitivity to a broad wavelength range to determine the ages of individual star clusters. NGC 4394 is one of 40 galaxies they studied in this way.

title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
summary: A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive.
content:

November 11
NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison

NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
October 26

Curtain
Toggle
2-Up
A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily.
Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency
reported
that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations.
The
OLI
(Operational Land Imager) on
Landsat 9
captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A
shortwave-infrared
signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating
pumice
stretches across the water in the same direction.
A false-color backscatter radar image from the
NISAR
(NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a
large disturbance
in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the
MODIS
(Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and
VIIRS
(Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s
volcanic plumes and infrared signature
.
Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16
confirming
the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the
bloodiest battles
in the history of the U.S. Marines.
The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
How long the new land will persist remains an open question. New land created by the 2023 eruption succumbed to wave action after just a few weeks, Slayback said. New land on volcanic islands has persisted more than a decade only a handful of times in recent times, including at Capelinhos, Surtsey, McDonald Island, and Home Reef, he added. “I imagine we’ll see this new land wash away within a few months,” he said. “But we’ll have to wait and see.”
Among the scientists watching closely is James Garvin, the chief scientist at Goddard and a geologist with a long-standing interest in how underwater volcanic eruptions create new islands and other landforms.
Typically,
tephra
-dominated eruptions like this form new land that is quickly “attacked” by ocean waves and other hydrologic forces, Garvin explained. An exception is when the eruption also injects certain types of lava that “cement” the ash into stronger material. “If we do see injection of basaltic-andesitic lava within the new materials, then it’s possible the new land could follow a pattern different from what we monitored in 2023,” he said.
NISAR will be especially valuable for tracking the site, Garvin said, because it makes frequent, high-resolution
interferometric
observations through clouds and can show whether the new land erodes, subsides, or grows. The satellite has already recorded major changes at the eruption site between
October 28 and November 11
.
NASA scientists will also analyze sub-meter-resolution imagery from commercial satellites through NASA’s
Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program
. These images can reveal subtle deformation features like rilles, fractures, and cracks that offer clues about the stability of the new land.
Both Slayback and Garvin have studied new volcanic land before. They were part of a team that monitored
new land
in the Kingdom of Tonga after an eruption in the Southwest Pacific but before most of it was obliterated during the highly explosive
Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai caldera collapse and eruption
in January 2022.

U.S. Geological Survey

title: NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution
summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb […]
content:
5 Min Read
NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star.
Credits:
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets.
This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals new details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
.
Image: Dust In Cassiopeia A (MIRI Image)
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star.
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)
Stars
begin
their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and
protostars
— infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun.
As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve, with increasingly heavier elements fusing in the core (eventually stopping at iron) and lighter elements fusing in surrounding layers. This leads to
multiple shells
of elements that provide a record of a star’s evolutionary history. When a star goes supernova, these elements are scattered into the surrounding space, where some of them condense to form dust grains, which can clump together. By studying and mapping the composition of these individual, solar-system-sized dust clumps in Cas A, Webb found evidence of a shell merger, a process in which the layers inside a star mix before the explosion.
“Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,” said Tea Temim, lead author of the
study
and research scientist from Columbia University in New York. “So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.”
Image: Dust In Cassiopeia A, North Up (MIRI)
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star.
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)
For the researchers to know where to look with Webb, they also leveraged data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope. Although it couldn’t resolve the minute details of the region during its
observation
, Spitzer identified three specific regions to observe with Webb’s keen eye.
Two of the targets were inside Cas A’s
reverse-shocked
region, where an inward-moving
shock wave
collides with debris thrown outward by the supernova. Webb observed that the ejecta in one of the two contained mostly silica dust, while the other was dominated by carbon dust. The third target was the “
Green Monster
,” a structure first discovered by Webb, which was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates. Unlike the other two regions, the Green Monster originated from material the star shed before it exploded, rather than from the supernova’s ejecta.
Image: Dust in Cassiopeia A (Spitzer and Webb)
NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope observed the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, helping to identify key regions that NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope later examined. Webb’s higher resolution provides finer details into the chemistry of the remnant’s dust.
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI), Alyssa Pagan (STScI)
Building on the X-ray observations of
NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory
and the
JAXA-led XRISM
, Webb mapped the dust composition of Cas A across the entire remnant, providing crucial insight into the shell merger phenomenon. Together, these observations indicate that the merger was underway very shortly before the supernova explosion.
“With Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,” said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. “As a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. It’s telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.”
The dust map from Webb also reveals that the merger signatures are present throughout much of the supernova remnant. These efforts provide a new method for other astronomers who want to infer characteristics about an originating star’s structure by using the dust of a supernova remnant.
The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
summary: A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
content:
The Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory is located on the west coast of Spitsbergen, an island in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, shown in this image acquired with the
OLI
(Operational Land Imager) on
Landsat 9
on July 30, 2026.
NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin
More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a
new, more precise method
for tracking satellites.
Since then,
satellite laser ranging
(SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the
Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory
—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.
In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system
officially debuted
at the
Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory
in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the
OLI
(Operational Land Imager) on
Landsat 9
in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.
While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s
Space Geodesy Project
. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.
The Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system fires at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, against a backdrop of aurora borealis on October 7, 2026.
NASA/Julie Horvath (KBR)
Years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.
Along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the
terrestrial reference frame
, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s
center of mass
, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as
GPS
, all rely on an accurate reference frame.
The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about
polar-orbiting
satellites, which include
ICESat-2
,
GRACE-FO
, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”
Certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz said.
Innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz said. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a
bird sanctuary
. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is currently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the
McDonald Geodetic Observatory
in Texas.

U.S. Geological Survey

title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
summary: Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang.
content:
Even as the
unusually quiet
2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On
November 15, 2026
, the Fiji Meteorological Service began
issuing updates
about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades.
Named
Xavier
, the system
intensified rapidly
, thriving in an environment with
minimal wind shear
and sea surface temperatures of
29 degrees
Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing
tropical cyclones
. Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only
Wati
, a short-lived storm that emerged in October.
As Xavier developed,
NASA satellite data
showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the
El Niño
that has been present in the region
since June
.
When the
MODIS
(Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s
Aqua
satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about
195 kilometers
(120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the
cyclone intensity scale
used in the region or a Category 4 on the
Saffir-Simpson scale
.
The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the
international date line
on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert
Phil Klotzbach
. Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically
shifts northeast
during El Niño years. Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an
unusually rapid pace
.
According to news reports, Xavier
damaged homes
and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa.
Xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the
Fiji Meteorological Service
projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line. Storm activity in the Southwest Pacific basin typically
peaks in February
.

title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
summary: Open data from NASA’s Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before.
content:
5 min read
NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars.
NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR)
An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A
paper describing the results
published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.
Using 15 years of data from NASA’s
Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.
A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.
“We don’t see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can’t just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from,” said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”
This artist’s concept shows a pulsar, which emits light in regular pulses as it rotates, like a cosmic lighthouse. Pulsars are dense remnants of exploded stars, and are part of a class of objects called neutron stars. Openly available data from NASA’s Fermi space telescope can help scientists spot pulsars in the gamma-ray spectrum.
NASA/JPL-Caltech
Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.
Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future
quantum computers
. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.
“We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data,” Gazith said.
Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.
The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.
“We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn’t find,” said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. “The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”
This view of the gamma-ray sky is constructed from one year of Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observations. The map shows the rate at which the LAT instrument detects gamma rays with energies above 300 million electron volts — about 120 million times the energy of visible light — from different sky directions. Brighter colors equal higher rates. Fermi’s openly available data archive contains a wealth of information that has supercharged scientific studies about the extreme universe.
NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration
The discovery would not have happened without NASA’s longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.
“The nice thing about NASA data is it’s all open,” Clark said. “All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.”
That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA’s
Fermitools
, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.
The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with new findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.
“Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search,” said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “It’s made all of the science better.”
For more information about NASA’s Fermi mission, visit:
https://www.nasa.gov/fermi
By Amanda Moon Adams

title: El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
summary: Winter precipitation helped wake dormant seeds in northern Chile, carpeting the desert with what may be the region’s most extensive flowering of the satellite era.

Parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, normally one of the driest places on Earth, turned red-purple, green, and white in austral spring 2026 following an unusually wet winter. The rain woke seeds lying dormant in the soil, setting off what scientists say may be the most extensive
desierto florido
, or “flowering desert,” of the satellite era.
The rains came as El Niño was strengthening in the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño, the subtropical Pacific high that normally keeps the region dry weakens, while a blocking high tends to form in the South Pacific near the tip of South America. Together, these shifts push the Southern Hemisphere storm track equatorward.
Beginning in mid-July, a series of storm fronts fed by an
atmospheric river
brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades to a long stretch of Chile, from the Atacama region south to Los Lagos,
according to Chile’s national weather service
(Dirección Meteorológica de Chile). In August, back-to-back winter storms blanketed parts of the Atacama Desert in
rare snow
.
The spring blooms that followed are visible in these satellite image pairs, which show the desert at different stages of flowering on September 14 (left) and on October 24 (right). The
OLI
(Operational Land Imager) on
Landsat 8
acquired the September images, and the OLI on
Landsat 9
acquired the October images.
The pair above shows a part of the desert about 30 kilometers (20 miles) southwest of Copiapó, near the eastern sector of Desierto Florido National Park. The red-purple areas prominent in the October 24 scene are vast blooms of pata de guanaco, most likely
Cistanthe longiscapa
or another
Cistanthe
species, according to Roberto Chávez, a remote sensing scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.
Patches of red-purple
Cistanthe
are visible during a bloom in the Atacama Desert, shown in this photograph taken on October 24, 2026.
Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.
Chávez and colleagues photographed the
Cistanthe
blooms (above) in the area that same day. They were in the field to study the bloom with satellite data, drones, and digital cameras. The project aims to use these data to map how the bloom’s biodiversity changes across space and over time, to inform land-use planners and conservation managers.
The pair below shows another part of the blooming desert, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Copiapó. It lies within a
priority area
of the desert cited for its biological significance, including the flowering landscape.

Cistanthe
is abundant here in the October view, but the September scene (left) reveals another desert beauty. The green areas capped with white are blooms of suspiros, or
Nolana
, probably
Nolana baccata
, according to Andres Moreira-Muñoz, a scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso who studies plant geography. The researchers photographed the
Nolana
-covered hillsides below on September 24, 2026.
White
Nolana
blankets a hillside in the Atacama Desert during a bloom, shown in this photograph taken on September 24, 2026.
Matías Pérez-Evens and Roberto O. Chávez/LabGRS-Instituto de Geografía- Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.
Satellite data have been key to understanding the Atacama’s blooms. A
2014
study used Landsat observations to map where flowering and fog-fed plants grow around the Copiapó dune field. And a
2019 study
used NASA’s long-term vegetation record to identify 13 Atacama Desert blooms between 1981 and 2015.
Compared with those past blooms, the 2026 event stands out. “This instance of the ‘blooming desert’ phenomenon appears to be the most significant to date—in terms of its extent, intensity, and duration,” Moreira-Muñoz said, “at least since we began using remote sensing.”

summary: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! content:
It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, we’re deeply grateful for your help.
Here are a few more messages of gratitude our scientists sent in to share with you.
Chihoko Cullens, principal investigator (PI) of the
Space Cloud Watch
project, said: “Thank you to
Pirjo Koski, Huub Eggen, and Brian Scott
! Pirjo posts beautiful Noctilucent Cloud photos and has introduced us to other cloud databases in the Netherlands. Huub goes beyond basic data requested by us and actively discusses his observations providing helpful insights. Brian contributes consistently and has provided us with useful time-lapse videos. All three volunteers have consistently provided much needed data and have contributed their time in developing our Field Guide that now helps new citizen scientists correctly identify and report their observations. We are grateful for their contributions.”
Ryan Scott from the
Open Science Data Repository Analysis Working Groups
(OSDR AWGs) project said:
“A cohort of high school students took NASA’s free Machine Learning for Space Biology
course and then kept working as citizen science volunteers. Guided by OSDR AWG members​ who also gave their time freely, they mined open-access retinal data from the International Space Station (ISS) Rodent Research-9 Mission in the
NASA Open Science Data Repository
and trained a machine learning ensemble that separates oxidative damage from cell death in the eyes of space-flown mice, now published in the scientific journal
npj Microgravity
:
Machine learning ensemble reveals distinct molecular pathways of retinal damage in spaceflown mice
. Every citizen science student co-author earned authorship, and many of those listed above started college this fall with a NASA publication already behind them. Thanks to
Aditi Adapala, Mushtaq Ali, Naomi Z. Chang, Sophie Cai, Margaret Hitt, Anishka Jain, Matthew Lin, MarcAnthony Paolieri Della Monica, Elior Paley, Rudransh Pathak, Shawnak Samaddar, Shriya Sawant, Zhihan Shi, Rohin Sood, Fabian P. Uribe, Maxwell Volkan,
and
Jessica Wu,
plus OSDR AWG members
Anna Lewkowicz, Sunny Narayanan, Daniya Thomas, Ethan Waisberg, Pinar Avci, Joshua Ong, Marshall Tabetah, Richard Barker, Lauren Sanders,
and
Xiao Wen ‘Vivien’ Mao.”
Kyra Shaw, project coordinator for
Snapshot Wisconsin
at the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, said: “Our team has a Thanksgiving thank-you message for Snapshot volunteer
Tim Sparks.
Tim has been a dedicated Snapshot Wisconsin volunteer for nearly 10 years. Tim went above and beyond these past two years by helping to pilot test protocols and then joining the full launch for a new initiative, the Snapshot Phenology Project. Joining a select group of volunteers, Tim set up and is maintaining extra equipment to measure snow depth, temperature, and sound recordings at his Snapshot trail camera site. Thank you, Tim, for joining in our events, sending in your favorite photos, and going the extra mile to make the Snapshot Phenology Project a success!”
Benjamin Fernando from the
Impact Flash!
project said: “Thank you to everyone who’s been sending in images of the Moon! A special thanks to
Joerg Tomczak,
who helped us with the Artemis II campaign!”
Rachael Mady from the
Chesapeake Water Watch
project said: “We are so thankful for all of our volunteers! Since 2021, volunteers have been with us every step of the way and have made Chesapeake Water Watch possible. The Chesapeake Bay is the nation’s largest estuary, and we had people all over submitting observations and helping us cross our 6,000 observation milestone this year. While the project may be wrapping up, the impact that our volunteers have on improving the health of the Bay will continue for years to come. Thanks for all that you do!”
Marc Kuchner, from the
Backyard Worlds: Planet 9
science team, said: “Thank you to
Prateek Singh
for creating new tools for astronomy and for helping us lead our Space Apps challenge! Thank you to
Bruce Baller
and
Katharina Doll
for sharing their lists of brown dwarf discoveries and for inspiring all of us! Thank you to
Frank Kiwy
for his latest batch of python tools – shared with everyone – that dig through Pan-STARRS, WISE, SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, CatWISE, and NSC DR2 data! Thank you to
Michiharu Hyogo
for keeping the new publications coming,
Hugo Durantini Luca, Jim Rabe, and Lisa Stiller
for helping keep us all connected,
Peter Jalowiczor
for traveling around the world in the snow, and to
Farid Cedeno
and
Martin Bilsing
for teaching others about our project!”
Emma Yates, PI of the
Ozone Where We Live
(OWWL) project, said:  “We have developed an amazing collaboration with Quest Science Center, a non-profit that among many other things supports high school students interested in the Earth’s climate. One of the aspects of Quest is to develop student-run studies by pairing high school students with mentors. summary: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. content:
7 Min Read
NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy.
Credits:
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler
Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.
“Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.”
Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy
In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy.
Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler
Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits.
“We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!”
“When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.”
This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system.
In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into
neutron stars
and
black holes
, explode as
supernovae
, produce ripples in space-time known as
gravitational waves
, and create millisecond
pulsars
.
Hitting “replay”
The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries.
The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname.
“It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.
Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter.
After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao’s core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said.
What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles.
Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist’s Concept)
Top to bottom, left to right: In this artist’s concept, the stars are surrounded by a dust shell pre-merger; the stars brightened and the companion star’s orbit began to slow as the larger star engulfed it; the eruption occurred; dust freely expands at the poles after the merger.
Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia)
Reconstructing what happened
While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they
published their first paper
right before the eruption in 2025.)
Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from
NASA’s retired NEOWISE
(Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the
Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER)
in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust.
When
NASA’s SPHEREx
(Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The
Zwicky Transient Facility
detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up.
In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations from
NASA’s now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory
and
NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope
in Hawaii. Webb’s observations were taken on Dec. 24, 2025, as part of a just-in-time
Director’s Discretionary Time program
.
New path for future research
The team’s analysis of Bao, formally known as AT 2025abao, offers an approach to reconstructing the events: They conducted their analysis and made observations of the stars’ merger in real time. That allowed them to measure how efficient common envelope evolution is. In other cases, astronomers have worked to carefully reverse-engineer events that may have happened hundreds or even millions of years ago.
The new finding comes about just as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to conduct vast
publicly available surveys
. Its
Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey
will yield a huge number of new transient events that could benefit from similar analyses. “There’s going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,” Karambelkar said.
This work is funded in part by a grant from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.
The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

summary: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge
Credit: NASA / David Lam
NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision.
Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027.
Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight.
“As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!”
Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both
radioisotope
and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable.
Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.
Judges Needed
NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers
website
.
The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.
Future Engineers
administers the challenge through a contract with the
NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation
within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.
To learn more about the challenge, visit:
https://www.nasa.gov/power-to-explore

NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission.
NASA
On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation.
Since 2012, NASA
Space Apps Challenge
has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries. The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration.
Participants join events organized by local volunteers to work in teams and address one of the challenges and submit their project before the deadline. Projects are then judged to determine 10 global winners, to be announced in January.
“The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.”
One of the local winning teams from NASA Space Apps Challenge NYC pose with volunteer local lead Nate Cooper.

4 Min Read
New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound.
Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes. By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun.
NASA/CXC/SAO/K.Arcand, SYSTEM Sounds (M. Russo, A. Santaguida
M82
The galaxy Messier 82 (M82) is called a starburst galaxy because stars are forming there at a rate tens or even hundreds of times higher than in our Milky Way galaxy. This stellar birth boom may be due to a collision with another galaxy in the past. Today, Chandra sees giant plumes of hot gas that are the byproduct of young, giant stars that quickly explode and other star formation activity. One of the new sonifications combines Chandra’s data with optical data from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, as well as infrared views from NASA’s James Webb and retired Spitzer space telescopes. The sonification of the three types of light begins with a radar-like scan that is louder where sources are brighter. The X-ray data is mapped to the highest range of frequencies heard. Infrared data is heard as a low drone plus plucked sounds, while the optical data turns into a range of musical pitches and textures.

Orion Nebula
One of the closest and busiest star formation regions to Earth is the Orion Nebula (visible just below the belt in the Orion constellation with a small telescope and dark skies). Chandra sees more than a thousand stars in this area that are very energetic and active in their infancy. In the sonified version of the Chandra data, these stars are twinkling sounds, while the diffuse X-ray emission is mapped to pure high tones. An infrared image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the raw material of dust and gas used to build these new stars, and its data is heard as lower musical tones, distorted string instruments, and a digital harp.

Carina Nebula
A portion of the Carina Nebula, another star formation region, is nicknamed the “Cosmic Cliffs” because of its spectacular structure seen in infrared by NASA’s Webb. Chandra also looks at this region, seeing through the dust and gas, and detects individual baby stars – which are turned into short string sounds in the sonification. A diffuse X-ray glow throughout the region has longer strings notes assigned to it. The nebula in the Webb data is mapped to a sustained sound, punctuated by other instruments to denote features like stars and ridges.

Rho Ophiuchi
Rho Ophiuchi is a striking star-forming cloud, filled with gas and stars of different sizes and ages. Chandra reveals infant stars that violently flare and produce X-rays. Infrared data from Webb provides views of the cloud’s regions of gas and dust. When this data is made audible, Chandra’s X-rays become high-pitched glassy tones, along with other sustained sounds to mark the appearance of extended bright sources. The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. There is a gap in the middle of the piece due to dark dust clouds that emit very little light.

Curiosity Blog, Sols 5070-5076: The Return of the Polygons
NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this image of a portion of the area in front of the rover, in which the return of the regular, well-expressed polygons captured several weeks ago can be seen. Curiosity used its Mast Camera (MastCam) to capture this image on Sol 5073, or Martian day 5,073 of the Mars Science Laboratory mission, at 15:45:05 UTC.
NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS
Written by Abigail Fraeman, Deputy Project Scientist, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 13, 2026
Curiosity’s past several weeks have been very focused on drilling and analysis of the
“Basque Lakes”
and
“Nazca”
samples. We learned a lot from those drilled samples, but it’s time to hit the Martian road again and resume our climb up Mount Sharp.
The Yardang unit
on the upper part of the mountain is calling! As we climb higher on Mount Sharp, we’ll continue to use many of our less resource intensive science instruments like APXS, ChemCam, MAHLI, and Mastcam to document the chemistry and textures of the rocks we encounter while making purposeful upward progress. These measurements allow us to document changes in the environments that formed the rocks and that altered them over time.
The two areas we explored this week had rocks that were crisscrossed by lots of small, regular sized polygons surrounded by raised ridges. This texture was very similar to
the rocks we encountered a few months ago slightly lower on the mountain
. Those unique textures really surprised us when we first saw them, and we’ve been spending time as a science team discussing how they may have formed. Polygonal textures like these can form under a variety of different conditions including shrinkage of the surface when water is lost from minerals, temperature cycling, or compaction and expansion after being buried and exposed. The data Curiosity collected this week give us more clues about the genesis of these features and what they reveal about the evolution of Mars’ habitability. We’ll also get information about the composition of the cements that form the raised ridges around the polygons.
In the orbital view of our future route, I can see the layers that we’ll reach next week or the week after have textures very similar to where we first saw the amazing field of polygons. So I’m guessing we’ll continue to encounter polygons in the next couple drives, and that they’ll look more dramatic and expansive with each drive. But this is just a guess! After over 5,000 sols of exploring with Curiosity I’ve learned Mars is full of surprises, so I’m really looking forward to seeing what’s up ahead in the new future and testing if my guess is correct.

title: Tossing Fireworks from Cloud to Cloud
summary: For many astronauts, the spectacular sight of lightning stands out when looking back at Earth from the International Space Station.
content:
October 28, 2026
For astronauts on the
International Space Station
, looking back to Earth at night can be as dazzling as looking outward toward the stars.
In an
essay for
Air & Space
magazine, Donald Pettit, a NASA astronaut and
dedicated photographer
, described the “spectacular” view of Earth at night visible from the station. Cities and civilization, he wrote, looked “like tendrils outlined with the glimmer of a Broadway marquee.” Intense, colorful lights cast by clusters of fishing boats across darkened oceans reminded him of “a constellation of stars” forming “unfamiliar members of the Zodiac.”
NASA astronaut
Sally Ride
—the first American woman to fly in space—also marveled at the “indescribable” sights of Earth from orbit. Lightning was among the most spectacular, she noted in
an essay for the same magazine
. “On Earth, people see lightning from below the clouds. In orbit, we see it from above,” she wrote. “Bolts of lightning are diffused by the clouds into bursting balls of light. Sometimes, when a storm extends hundreds of miles, it looks like a transcontinental brigade is tossing fireworks from cloud to cloud.”
All three phenomena—city lights, fishing fleets, and lightning—were on display when the space station passed over the South China Sea near Borneo at 14:20 UTC (9:20 p.m. Western Indonesian Time) on October 28, 2026. When an astronaut captured this scene with a
Nikon Z9 camera
, several
overshooting tops
bubbled up from thunderstorms, including two illuminated by lightning flashes. These tall, domelike protrusions rise above a thunderstorm’s
anvil
and sometimes into the stratosphere, indicating strong updrafts and intense storms.
The lights of
Singapore
, a city-state of
6.2 million people
, appear on the left side of the image, with the curving Singapore Strait separating the city from Batam and Bintan islands to the south. The cluster of blue lights west of Singapore, reminiscent of the
Pleiades
, or Seven Sisters, was likely produced by
fishing boats
using bright lights to attract squid or schooling fish such as sardines or anchovies. Offshore to the northwest, the scattered orange points are likely
gas flares
.
For many astronauts, it’s the sight of lightning that lingers. “Like fireflies in the night, lightning is my favorite sight from space,” said NASA astronaut Anil Menon in a video of Earth’s darkened limb that he
posted on X
, where pinpoints of lightning flicker almost constantly. Lightning is hard to capture and share, he added, but the video offers the best representation he’s seen. “It’s unchanged, at real speed, and shows the vast reach of storms and lightning across earth, plus the rapid flashes that dance across the horizon.”
NASA scientists estimate
that there are
2,000 thunderstorms
occurring on Earth at any one moment, producing nearly 60 flashes per second—roughly 5 million flashes per day.
Astronaut photograph
ISS075-E-250951
was acquired on October 28, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the
Expedition 75 crew
. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The
International Space Station Program
supports the laboratory as part of the
ISS National Lab
to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the Internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC
Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth
.

title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
summary: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University Date: Nov. 16, 2026 During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in […]
content:
2 min read
Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
NASA’s Perseverance rover captured this image of a bright, silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using its left Mastcam-Z camera on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 13:03:53.
NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU
Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University
Date: Nov. 16, 2026
During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the
igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated.
Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.
Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?
When Perseverance previously encountered
silica-rich rocks on the inner rim
of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.
A close-up image of a silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using the Perseverance rover’s SHERLOC WATSON camera, located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm. This image was acquired on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 17:33:55.

title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
summary: Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.
content:
1988
2026
A false-color satellite image from 1988 shows mountain ridges of Indonesia’s Sudirman Range. Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green.
NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin
A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988.
NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

A false-color satellite image from 1988 shows mountain ridges of Indonesia’s Sudirman Range. Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green.
NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin
A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988.
